parts.partTitle: Why Raw Futures & Callback Hell Break Async Java

beats.headline: Sequential HTTP calls stack latency into slow APIs.
beats.subline: Calling future.get() parks your thread, and nested callbacks turn code sideways.
beats.narration: Sequential backend calls add every downstream latency together into a slow response. Calling raw Future get parks the caller thread, while nested completion handlers shatter your control flow and error handling.

beats.title: Nested Callbacks vs. CompletableFuture DAG

top.label: Nested Callback Hell

bottom.label: CompletableFuture Pipeline
points: Declarative stages form a clean directed graph
Exceptions automatically flow to end handlers

beats.narration: Nested callbacks obscure the happy path and force manual exception forwarding. CompletableFuture replaces callbacks with a clean directed graph where stages transform data and exceptions flow naturally to end handlers.

beats.title: Creating CompletableFutures Correctly

steps.explanation: Starts background task returning a result value, explicitly bound to a dedicated thread pool.
Executes background Runnable for side-effects or fire-and-forget tasks returning Void.
Returns an already-completed future, ideal for short-circuiting cache hits without thread switching.

beats.narration: Use supplyAsync for background tasks returning values and runAsync for side effects. Always supply an explicit pool, and use completedFuture for instant cache returns with zero thread context switching.

beats.title: Async Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)
beats.subtitle: Declarative pipeline execution flow

nodes.label: Fan-Out Tasks
nodes.detail: Profile, Pricing & Stock run on I/O Pool

beats.narration: Incoming requests fan out into parallel background tasks on an I/O pool. Stages transform data declaratively, while timeouts and recovery handlers route failure paths into safe default responses.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
takeaways: Future get blocks threads; callbacks nest sideways
Use completedFuture for zero-cost cache returns

parts.partTitle: thenApply vs thenCompose & The commonPool Trap

beats.headline: Omitting the Executor parameter can stall your JVM.
beats.subline: Blocking HTTP calls inside ForkJoinPool.commonPool starve all parallel features.
beats.narration: Omitting the executor in supplyAsync defaults to ForkJoinPool commonPool. In a container with two CPUs, just three blocking network calls freeze background processing across your entire JVM.

beats.title: thenApply vs. thenCompose

bottom.label: thenCompose (FlatMap)
points: Flattens nested futures into single CompletableFuture<R>

beats.narration: Use thenApply when your mapping function returns a normal value, just like Stream map. Use thenCompose when your function returns another CompletableFuture to flatten the nested result into a single stage.

beats.title: Chaining Dependent Async Pipelines

steps.explanation: Avoids double-wrapped CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<AccountCredit>> by flattening downstream stage.
Transforms UserProfile to String email synchronously in-place.

beats.narration: Passing an async function into thenCompose flattens the result into a single future. Using thenApply there instead creates a double-wrapped future that requires awkward manual unwrapping.

beats.title: The ForkJoinPool.commonPool() Starvation Trap
beats.subtitle: Blocking I/O exhausts available CPU workers
beats.narration: By default, commonPool creates only CPU-count minus one workers. Blocking those workers on socket reads queues up parallel streams and async tasks across your entire JVM.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
takeaways: thenApply maps values; thenCompose flattens futures
Never execute blocking I/O on ForkJoinPool.commonPool
Isolate CPU and I/O tasks on dedicated Executors

parts.partTitle: Combining Futures: thenCombine, allOf & anyOf Gotchas

beats.headline: CompletableFuture allOf does not cancel on failure.
beats.subline: If one task fails in 10ms, allOf still waits 2 seconds for every slow task to finish.
beats.narration: CompletableFuture allOf creates a barrier for multiple tasks. But if one task fails in ten milliseconds, allOf still waits two seconds for every other task to complete before throwing an exception.

beats.title: Fanning In N Futures with allOf

steps.explanation: Creates barrier returning CompletableFuture<Void> that triggers when all input futures finish.
Calling join inside thenApply does not block because all input futures are already complete.

beats.narration: Pass an array of futures to allOf to build a barrier. Then attach thenApply and call join on each input future to collect typed results without blocking any thread.

beats.title: Combining Operators Comparison

top.label: thenCombine vs. allOf
points: allOf builds barrier for N dynamic tasks

bottom.label: anyOf Gotcha
points: Does not auto-cancel losing in-flight futures

beats.narration: Use thenCombine for two futures and allOf for dynamic collections. Watch out for anyOf: the first finished future wins even if it failed, and slower tasks keep running in background threads.

beats.title: Tracing anyOf Exception Behavior
beats.caption: Fastest response wins—even when it is a failure!

lines.text: # Server launches hedged requests to Replica A and Replica B
[40ms] Replica B succeeded with valid data (ignored!)

beats.narration: Look at this terminal log. Replica A failed in five milliseconds with a socket exception. Because anyOf completes on the first response, it returns that failure immediately while Replica B succeeds ignored.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In
takeaways: thenCombine merges two concurrent futures cleanly
allOf barrier requires thenApply + join to collect results
anyOf completes on first result, including errors

parts.partTitle: Async Exception Handling, Timeouts & Virtual Threads

beats.headline: Exceptions inside futures bypass standard try-catch blocks.
beats.subline: Uncaught errors skip transformation stages until explicit recovery hooks catch them.
beats.narration: Exceptions thrown inside a future bypass outer try-catch blocks completely. They skip downstream transformation stages silently until an explicit recovery stage intercepts them.

beats.title: Error Handling: exceptionally vs handle vs whenComplete

top.label: exceptionally & handle
points: exceptionally recovers normal flow on failure
handle receives both result and exception

bottom.label: whenComplete
points: Cannot modify result or swallow exceptions
Ideal for metrics, logging, and audit tracking

beats.narration: Use exceptionally to return fallback values on failure, and handle to transform outcomes regardless of success or error. Use whenComplete strictly for side effects like metrics without altering pipeline output.

beats.title: Non-Blocking Timeouts & Exception Recovery

steps.explanation: Triggers TimeoutException if stage does not complete within specified deadline duration.
Completes normally with fallback value if upstream takes longer than timeout window.
Unwraps CompletionException to inspect true root cause error message.

beats.narration: Java 9 introduced non-blocking timeouts with orTimeout and completeOnTimeout. When catching errors in exceptionally, always check ex getCause to unwrap the underlying CompletionException wrapper.

beats.title: Modern Java 21+ Async Architecture
beats.subtitle: Combining CompletableFuture with Virtual Threads

nodes.label: Semaphore Capping
nodes.detail: Limits max concurrent external service calls

beats.narration: In Java 21, pass a Virtual Thread Executor to supplyAsync for blocking I/O tasks. Pair it with a Semaphore to cap downstream concurrency without thread pool sizing bottlenecks.

beats.title: Chapter Complete! Run the Lab
takeaways: Use exceptionally & handle for recovery; whenComplete for logging
Enforce deadlines with Java 9 orTimeout & completeOnTimeout
Java 21 Virtual Threads remove pool sizing bottlenecks
